extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental chemists (17th‑century learned readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for assessing arguments and experiments that claim certain 'elements' or 'principles' compose mixed bodies — e.g., how to design, interpret, and defend experimental demonstrations and theoretical accounts of elemental composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define what is meant by 'Element' or 'Principle'
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay down what should be all along understood by the word Principle or Element; Carneades and company agree to use 'Elements' and 'Principles' as equivalent terms for 'those primitive and simple Bodies of which the mixt ones are said to be composed, and into which they are ultimately resolved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and fix terminology at the outset so disputants know what is being claimed. Avoid pointless word‑wrangling, but be explicit about the working definition used in experiments and arguments. Example anti‑pattern: arguing about counts of 'elements' without first specifying what counts as an 'element'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiments/phenomena over captious dialectical subtleties
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wiser to insist on phenomena relating to the question, provided by experiments, than on Dialectical subtleties which often 'declare the wit of him that uses them, then increase the knowledge or remove the doubts of sober lovers of truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing claims about composition, prioritize clear experimental observations and phenomena rather than intricate syllogisms that may confuse rather than inform. Anti‑pattern: substituting rhetorical logical tricks for empirical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use obvious, sensible experiments rather than far‑fetched demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments to prove obvious truths should not be 'farr fetch'd'; obvious and easy analyses are more suitable to the nature of the doctrine being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, reproducible experiments that the senses can verify. Avoid overly elaborate constructions meant to impress but not to reveal reliably the substances involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show that separated products were pre‑existent (pre‑existence requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: An analysis that produces substances (e.g., 'fire' and 'water' from burning wood) must demonstrate that those substances were pre‑existent in the compound; it is not enough that the analyzer yields certain products — one must prove the products were present before analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments or controls to distinguish whether an analyzer (like fire) merely generates new products or reveals pre‑existing ingredients. Anti‑pattern: assuming that products of an analysis equal the original constituents without independent evidence of pre‑existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept analysis by one method (fire) as universally authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: Question the right of fire to be the proper and universal instrument of analysing mixt bodies, since fire may not only separate ingredients but also alter or produce new substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test multiple modes of analysis and be cautious about conclusions based solely on thermal decomposition. Provide evidence that the analyst (e.g., fire) does not itself create or significantly transform supposed ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalising elemental counts from single or very few experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on one or a few experiments to establish the number of elements (e.g., the Peripatetick four or Chymical three) is insufficient; hypotheses built on two or three experiments are easily overturned by further trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate many diverse experiments before concluding an elemental count. Anti‑pattern: treating a single neat demonstration as definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check consistency across different materials (cross‑material sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid account of elements should apply across a range of bodies: some substances (gold, silver, certain minerals) resist reduction into the proposed number of heterogeneous substances, while others yield more or fewer than that number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims by attempting reductions on many different classes of material (metals, animal/vegetable substances, minerals). A genuine elemental theory should explain or admit exceptions; lack of universality is a weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reproducible recoverability of original substances
rubrics_metrics.description: When a corpuscle or metal (e.g., gold, quicksilver) is disguised in compounds, the ability to recover the same numerical, fixed, ponderous metal afterwards supports the claim that it was a genuine constituent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recoverability (reversibility) as evidence that a component survived combination and was not merely the product of the analysis. Example: recover original gold or mercury from varied compounds to support its status as a principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate argument (proof) from rhetoric (eloquence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical flourishes or 'harangues' do not substitute for argumentative proof; Carneades declines to treat the rhetorical part as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the argumentative content independently of style. Anti‑pattern: letting eloquence of presentation stand in for experimental or logical substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value theoretical coherence with wider philosophical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine gains plausibility when it coheres with other parts of philosophy; Aristotle's account is defended insofar as its notions are curiously adapted into one system and mutually support one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a proposed elemental theory integrates with other established principles and phenomena. Coherence is evidence (not proof) — but must be complemented by empirical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer ingredients from emergence alone (creation vs separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments where fire yields products, it may appear those products are made out of the concrete rather than that the concrete was made up of those products; thus one must not infer constituent status from mere emergence under analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide arguments or controls showing the direction of dependence (components → compound) rather than assuming compound → components. Anti‑pattern: confusing decomposition products with original constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on obscure 'substantial forms' to explain textures/qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking a substantial Form to explain the origin of textures and qualities is unsatisfactory if that Form's own origin is more obscure than the phenomena it is supposed to explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mechanistic or corpuscular explanations (e.g., size/shape/cohesion of particles) over opaque metaphysical postulates unless those postulates are independently evidenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ corpuscular hypotheses (bulk and figure) to explain variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning peculiar size and shape to corpuscles of each supposed element can plausibly account for the enormous variety of compound bodies produced from a small number of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use particle‑scale hypotheses (shape, size, clustering) as legitimate explanatory devices to account for texture and property variation; test implications experimentally where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles should be both clear and solid (clarity and robustness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles ought 'to be like Diamonds, as well very clear, as perfectly solid' — i.e., intelligible and strongly supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand that proposed elements/principles be clearly intelligible (definition and explanation) and robust to scrutiny (empirical support and coherence). Anti‑pattern: hypotheses that are obscure in meaning or fragile under counter‑experiment.
